On 16 April 1853 the first passenger train in India ran from Bori Bunder in Bombay to Thane, about 34 kilometres away. It was run by the Great Indian Peninsula Railway, carried some 400 guests and was pulled by three engines named Sahib, Sultan and Sindh.

Steam railways had begun in Britain with lines such as the Liverpool and Manchester Railway in 1830. Private British companies built India's lines with a profit guaranteed by the colonial government. The governor general, Lord Dalhousie, pushed for a national network in 1853, for trade, for moving troops and for carrying raw cotton to the ports.

Lines spread fast. Within fifty years they joined the main cities and ports, and later reached hill stations like Darjeeling on the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway. Railways moved grain into famine areas, but also out of them, and carried pilgrims, migrants and nationalist ideas.

Bori Bunder became the great Gothic station now called Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus. Today Indian Railways is one of the largest networks and employers in the world.
